description: We are AERVYX, a team of Engineers from Wright State University. Our project uses AI and NASA data to discover scientific opportunities on Mars and optimize astronaut exploration routes. We bring skills in engineering, programming, data analysis, optimization, and biomedical research. We welcome participants interested in AI, aerospace, planetary science, and software development.
summary:
AERVYX is a concept design for an AI-powered Mars exploration platform. It combines public NASA orbital data to help scientists and mission planners find promising science targets, judge the terrain around them, and compare possible routes for an astronaut on foot. In our interactive demo, AERVYX is shown as the AI built into the astronaut’s helmet: it displays the map, marks hazards such as boulders, and scans anything unusual the crew finds, flagging possible targets for scientist review.

The Martian Map challenge asks for a way to understand and move across Martian terrain. AERVYX turns NASA imagery and elevation data into a map-based tool that shows where an astronaut could go, how steep and demanding each route is, and which places may be worth studying.

It matters because safer, better-planned surface trips could save crew time and effort and help scientists spend that time at the most promising locations.
details:
What it does and how it works
AERVYX is a concept design for an AI-powered Mars exploration platform. It helps scientists and mission planners find promising science targets, judge the terrain around them, and compare routes for an astronaut on foot. The planning workflow has three steps: (1) explore imagery, elevation and slope layers and pick a possible target; (2) analyze the terrain around each site, with every candidate marked “not verified”; (3) set limits such as maximum slope, crew workload and science priority, and compare three routes by distance, steepness and estimated effort. In our interactive demo, AERVYX is also the AI built into the astronaut’s helmet. It shows the map, marks hazards such as boulders, and scans anything unusual the crew finds, then flags possible science targets for scientist review. The proposed method is simple: elevation data gives slope and roughness, a search over the terrain finds routes under the planner’s limits, and candidate sites are flagged for expert review. The demo runs this on synthetic stand-in terrain generated in the browser. All rankings, route numbers and scan results are illustrative, not mission findings.

Benefits and intended impact
AERVYX gives a clearer view of terrain, a side-by-side comparison of route options, and a clear separation between possible discoveries and verified findings. The intended impact is smarter, safer and more productive surface exploration: less wasted crew time and effort, safer route choices, and more science time at the most promising locations.

Tools and technology
HTML, CSS and JavaScript with WebGL2 (interactive demo and 3D walk view); Python with NumPy, OpenCV, Pillow and scikit-image (synthetic terrain and illustrations); PptxGenJS (slide deck); Kokoro text-to-speech with sherpa-onnx (demo narration voices); Playwright and FFmpeg (testing); Claude (AI assistant for drafting and code). It runs in a web browser and needs no special hardware.

What makes it creative
Instead of a static map, AERVYX puts the AI where the astronaut is, in the helmet, so the same tool that plans the route also marks hazards and scans finds as the crew walks. The demo has a guided tour, a first-person walk on Mars, and a scripted rock scan that hands off to a science team. We also built honesty into the design: unverified targets are always labeled, the AI does not claim to have found life, and a fictional alien scene is clearly marked as fiction.

Factors we considered
Astronaut safety and workload (the team combines industrial and systems engineering with biomedical engineering), scientific caution so discoveries stay separate from verified findings, and transparency about AI use. This is a concept design. It is not yet connected to live NASA data, and a future version would use real terrain data with scientist review.
